By 2031, AI will fluently perform the calculation, data-analysis, and even much of the presentation-drafting this course currently teaches by hand, and task-exposure research's finding that programming and writing skills are positively associated with exposure applies directly to these deliverables. Foundational scaffolding caps the rating at Medium regardless of capability gains, since the constraint is structural rather than task-based. The rating holds Medium; the genuine uncertainty is how much of the course's content delivery shifts toward AI-assisted exploration versus how much survives as unaided student work, not whether the course's role as curricular entry point and design-process foundation remains necessary for students continuing in engineering technology.
EET 1040.d: This course is an introductory engineering course exposing students to a cross section of topics in contemporary civil, electrical and mechanical engineering disciplines to assist them with their education career choices. Students are taught to work in teams, introduced to the design process, utilize math and computer programs to analyze raw data and properly display their results in a presentation to their peers. The history of the engineering profession and its relation to current national, social, industrial, ethical, and international issues and problems will be discussed.

r: Circuits I covers DC analysis, mesh and nodal methods, Thevenin and Norton conversion, power, magnetism, capacitance, and inductance, plus an introduction to electrical laboratory procedure and measurement of basic circuit parameters. The analytical work, solving linear circuit equations, is squarely inside AI's demonstrated competence; task-exposure research classifies this kind of well-structured quantitative problem as highly exposed. But this is the entry course of the entire EET circuits sequence, and its lab component requires students to measure real components and reconcile bench readings against calculated predictions, a verification task that needs the trained human, not just the correct formula. Given the ABET-relevant engineering-technology sequence and foundational prerequisite role feeding directly into Circuits II and beyond, the instrumental need to build this base competence is not eroded at 24 months. The rating holds Low.

By 2031, AI will solve DC circuit problems and simulate mesh and nodal networks fluently, eroding the rationale for students to grind through hand calculation. But the laboratory half of the course, measuring real resistance, capacitance, and inductance and reconciling discrepancies between prediction and bench reading, still requires a human who understands the underlying physics, a genuine verification burden with practical safety implications for later coursework involving live circuits. Foundational scaffolding is decisive here: as the first course in the EET sequence, Circuits I underlies Circuits II, electronics, and digital circuits, and the ABET-relevant credit-hour structure keeps it in place across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium: hand analysis increasingly automates, but the measurement-verification competence and gatekeeping foundational role for the entire major keep the course instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI performs circuit analysis and simulation essentially without friction, and the case for teaching hand computation as the primary skill is largely eroded under a central capability trajectory. What survives is the foundational and verification core: EET students still need to build basic hardware-measurement competence and the intuition to catch when a calculation and a bench reading disagree, since diagnosing that gap is exactly the non-obvious-failure condition verification burden describes. As the entry point for the whole circuits-and-electronics sequence, the course's structural role does not depend on capability alone. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational scaffolding and verification burden. The open question is how much of the analytical content shifts to AI-assisted exploration around a preserved measurement core, not whether the entry-level foundational course remains necessary for the technology curriculum.
EET 1140.d: This course covers DC circuit analysis, including mesh analysis, nodal analysis, Thevenin conversion, Norton conversion, power, magnetism and magnetic circuits, capacitance, and inductance. An introduction to electrical laboratory procedures and the measurement of basic circuit parameters is also included.

This is dense, well-structured quantitative reasoning, exactly the kind of task observed-usage data shows concentrated in Computer and Mathematical categories. But the course sits at the center of the EET curriculum and, like its predecessor, pairs analysis with measurement; interpreting frequency-response or impedance behavior on real hardware and reconciling it against phasor predictions requires the trained human. Within the ABET-relevant sequence and as the gateway to electronics and digital-circuits coursework, the instrumental need to build this analytical-plus-hardware competence is intact at 24 months. By 2031, AI will handle AC circuit analysis, phasor computation, and frequency-response prediction fluently, weakening the rationale for students to perform this by hand, task-exposure research consistently finds structured quantitative work among the categories most affected by adoption. What remains load-bearing is measurement and hardware verification: real RLC circuits, transformers, and two-port networks behave in ways that diverge from ideal models, and diagnosing that gap is a genuine verification task with downstream safety relevance for electronics work. Foundational scaffolding for the whole EET sequence and the ABET-relevant credit-hour structure cap the erosion at Medium regardless of how capable analytical tools become. The rating rises to Medium: phasor-based computation increasingly automates, but hardware-verification competence and the course's gateway role into electronics and digital circuits keep it instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI performs AC circuit analysis and network modeling with high fluency, and the hand-computation rationale for the course is substantially eroded in a central-case scenario, consistent with the fast doubling of AI task-time-horizons observed in recent capability trends. But electrical-engineering-technology work remains partly embodied: building, measuring, and troubleshooting real AC circuits and diagnosing when predicted and observed behavior diverge is not a task that gets delegated away, and the ABET-relevant sequence structure persists absent accreditor change. The rating holds Medium, capped jointly by foundational scaffolding and verification burden. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the analytical workload shifts to AI-assisted tools around a preserved measurement-and-troubleshooting core, not whether foundational AC-circuit competence remains instrumentally required for students continuing through the accredited electrical-engineering-technology curriculum.
EET 1150.d: This course is a continuation of EET 1140, using trigonometry and complex algebra. Studies include single-time constant circuits, phasors, and the j operator, RLC circuits with sinusoidal, steady-state sources, impedance and admittance, AC formulation of classic network theorems, complex network equations, complex power, frequency response, transformers, and two-port network models.

The uncertainty here is compounded by the description's brevity: without more detail on the balance of lecture, machine demonstration, and lab content, confidence in the precise task mix is lower than for the primary EET circuits sequence, though the structural, prerequisite-driven case for Medium is comparatively firm.
EET 2000.d: This course introduces electric circuits for non-EET majors. It covers DC and AC circuits, generators, motors, transformers, elementary electronic devices, and circuits.

r: Electronics covers the theory, modeling, and application of semiconductor devices, diodes, bipolar junction transistors, MOSFETs, thyristors, and operational amplifiers, with students learning to integrate them into filtering, amplification, and oscillation circuits. Device modeling and circuit-design calculation are well-structured quantitative tasks that observed-usage data shows concentrated among AI's most-adopted categories, and a model can readily generate a filter or amplifier topology on request. But applying that design to a real device with non-ideal parameters, biasing constraints, and thermal behavior requires judgment a human must verify, and the course is foundational scaffolding feeding directly into its co-requisite laboratory and later analog-electronics work in the ABET-relevant sequence. EET 2145.d: Students in this course will study the theory, modeling and application of semiconductor based electronic circuits. Devices studied include: diodes, bipolar junctions transistors, MOS field effect transistors, thyristors and operational amplifiers. The student will learn to integrate electronic devices in applications such as filtering, amplification, and oscillation.

r: This one-credit lab develops the hands-on skills to integrate semiconductor devices into filtering, amplification, and oscillation circuits, translating the co-requisite Electronics lecture into practical, bench-based exercises. AI can suggest a circuit topology, but it cannot solder a component, probe a live signal, or diagnose a cold joint. EET 2165.d: The student will develop the laboratory skills necessary for integration of electronic devices in applications such as filtering, amplification, and oscillation. The student will integrate the lecture content of EET2145 in the practical, hands-on laboratory exercises developed in this course.

Flip-flops, memories, analog-to-digital (ADC) and digital-to-analog converters (DAC) are used to design simple digital circuits. Computer architecture is introduced.

At 24 months AI already writes competent introductory C and LabVIEW code, but the instrumental need for students to acquire this programming foundation persists for now.

By 2031, AI coding assistants will handle most routine C implementation and LabVIEW instrument-panel construction, consistent with productivity research showing large speed gains for assisted coding work. The write-it-yourself rationale for this course weakens substantially. What remains necessary is the conceptual foundation for specifying, reading, and debugging AI-generated code and virtual-instrument logic, a verification competence the jagged-frontier evidence suggests matters most exactly where errors are non-obvious. Because this foundational programming literacy still feeds later data-acquisition and capstone work, the erosion is capped at Medium rather than reaching High. The rating rises to Medium: the digital, non-embodied nature of the work offers no protection, and the ABET-relevant sequence and foundational role only partially restrain a task category the evidence treats as highly automatable.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating the substantial majority of routine C and LabVIEW code, with the programmer's role shifting toward specification, integration, and validation. The instrumental case for manual implementation is largely eroded by 2036. Foundational programming and instrumentation literacy remains necessary, though, both because later data-acquisition and project work in the Advanced Manufacturing sequence depend on it and because verifying AI-generated measurement code carries real consequences when it feeds physical instrumentation. The rating holds Medium, restrained from High by that residual foundational and verification role rather than by embodiment, which offers no protection here. The genuine uncertainty is how programming instruction itself is restructured under ubiquitous AI coding tools, not whether some foundational competence remains instrumentally required.
EET 3380.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. C programming plus LabVIEW virtual-instrument construction course whose outcome is writing routine engineering code. Stanford's August 2026 payroll update places software developers and computer programmers in the most AI-exposed occupations, where employment of 22-to-25-year-olds is 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put computer programmers at -7.3%. Both are descriptive signals, not proof that AI caused the decline. No rating changed, because institutional lock-in and foundational-course caps already binds.
EET 3380.d: This is an upper-level programming course using the C programming language and National Instruments Lab View virtual instrumentation software. Methods for solving engineering problems using the C programming language are studied. The use of Lab View for the creation of virtual instrumentation in simulations and data acquisition is introduced.

r: This course develops communication-systems theory: information theory and channel capacity, A/D and D/A conversion, AM/FM and digital modulation, noise and quantization, and transmission-line analysis including Smith Charts. The work is predominantly analytical and computational, mapping to Analyzing Data or Information and Interacting With Computers, and AI systems already solve modulation and channel-capacity problems capably, placing this content among the more exposed engineering-theory categories. The course nonetheless feeds EET 3670's measurement sequence and sits inside the ABET-relevant electrical-engineering-technology curriculum, which mandates the subject area rather than this specific course. At 24 months the instrumental need to build communications-theory fluency is largely intact: AI can compute a link budget or a Smith Chart solution, but the conceptual grounding needed for the measurement and troubleshooting work that follows is not something a student acquires by watching AI solve problems.

By 2031, AI will fluently solve and explain communications-theory problems, channel capacity calculations, modulation analysis, transmission-line matching, weakening the work-it-by-hand rationale considerably, consistent with fast capability growth in quantitative reasoning tasks. The instrumental case shifts toward conceptual understanding needed to specify systems correctly and to interpret AI-assisted analysis, particularly since a plausible-looking but wrong transmission-line solution is a costly, non-obvious failure mode. Foundational scaffolding for the measurement sequence that follows, and the ABET-relevant curricular structure, cap the erosion at Medium. The rating rises from Low to Medium: theoretical computation is increasingly AI-deliverable, but the conceptual substrate remains necessary for the applied measurement work and troubleshooting judgment the program builds toward. The genuine uncertainty is how quickly employers in the communications sector actually adopt these AI analysis tools in daily practice, since diffusion of new capability into applied engineering workflows still lags the underlying model's raw ability by a meaningful margin at this horizon.

A decade out, AI is plausibly a capable communications-theory tutor and problem-solver across most of this content, and the computational-execution rationale is substantially eroded. But communications engineering technologists must still verify that a specified system will actually work, a task with real error costs when an AI-generated design carries a subtle transmission-line or noise-budget mistake, and this course's conceptual foundation feeds directly into the measurement and troubleshooting coursework built on top of it. The ABET-relevant sequence persists in the central case through 2036. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role and verification burden rather than rising to High. The uncertainty concerns how communications theory is taught under ubiquitous AI solvers, not whether the underlying conceptual competence remains instrumentally necessary downstream.
EET 3620.d: This course is an introduction to communication systems. Topics include: information theory, channel capacity, A/D and D/A techniques, modulation (AM, FM, and digital), noise sources, quantization, and transmission lines including Smith Charts.

r: Students in this course perform bench measurements on real communication circuits, signal-to-noise ratio, noise figure, impedance and admittance, phase, power, frequency, and spectrum analysis, including high-frequency field measurements. This is embodied, instrument-driven work: operating spectrum analyzers and RF test equipment, interpreting live readings, and diagnosing discrepancies between prediction and bench reality, which task-exposure research places well outside AI's current reach given its physical, hands-on character. AI can help compute expected SNR or noise-figure values, but it cannot operate the equipment or judge a live spectrum-analyzer trace. Verifying that a communications circuit actually performs as specified demands the trained student's own measurement judgment, a genuine error-cost concern in RF work. At 24 months the instrumental need to build hands-on measurement competence is essentially untouched by current AI capability.

By 2031, AI-assisted analysis will likely help interpret spectrum data and automate some measurement post-processing, but the core embodied competence, physically operating RF test instrumentation, calibrating setups, and reading live measurements under real-world noise and interference, is not something a language or reasoning model performs. Verification remains central: a misread noise-figure measurement or a miscalibrated setup has real downstream consequences for a communications system, keeping the trained human necessary at the bench. The ABET-relevant curricular structure and this course's role in the communications-technology sequence hold it in place across a catalog cycle. The instrumental case stays largely intact; AI augments the analysis layer, not the hands-on measurement act itself, and adoption of AI-assisted test benches in industry remains uneven, consistent with survey evidence that AI diffusion into firms still trails raw model capability.

Over a decade, more measurement automation and remote instrumentation will likely appear in industrial RF test environments, and some post-processing will further automate. But the pedagogical function here, a student personally developing the physical technique and calibrated judgment to operate and troubleshoot real RF measurement equipment, is not eliminated by that trend, and embodiment keeps direct substitution low through 2036 in the central case. The ABET-relevant sequence and the course's specialized, hands-on character persist. The rating stays Low; the most plausible shift is in how much simulated versus physical measurement time students get, not in whether the embodied measurement competence itself remains instrumentally necessary for the communications-technology track, a distinction that matters more as automated tools grow more capable elsewhere in the profession.
EET 3670.d: Students learn to perform measurements on communication circuits, including SNR, noise figure, impedance, admittance, phase, power, frequency, spectrum analysis, and fields at high frequencies.

r: Fiber Optics combines ray-propagation theory and emitter/detector analysis with the physical craft of connectorization and the study of fiber-based systems including FDDI and SONET. The theoretical portion, analyzing light propagation and system budgets, is moderately exposed to AI, mapping to Analyzing Data or Information. But connectorization is manual, embodied craft work: physically splicing, polishing, and testing fiber connections, an activity task-exposure research places in low-exposure physical-execution categories. Verifying that a fiber link actually meets loss and bandwidth specifications requires hands-on measurement judgment developed through direct practice, not a description of the procedure. The course sits within the ABET-relevant electrical-engineering-technology sequence, which mandates the subject area rather than this specific course. At 24 months the instrumental need to build both the theoretical and hands-on fiber competence is essentially intact.

By 2031, AI will fluently handle link-budget calculations and system-design analysis for fiber networks, eroding that portion of the course's rationale. The connectorization craft, however, a physical skill requiring dexterity, careful technique, and real-time quality judgment about a completed splice or connector, remains outside what AI performs on a student's behalf. Verifying a working fiber link against specification is a bench task with real consequences for telecom infrastructure reliability, keeping the trained human necessary. The ABET-relevant curricular structure holds the course in place across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low: the theoretical layer is increasingly AI-deliverable, but the embodied craft and verification core of the course are not, and adoption of automated splicing or testing equipment across the telecom sector remains far from universal at this horizon.

A decade out, AI will be a highly capable fiber-system design assistant, and automated testing equipment may absorb more diagnostic work in industrial settings. But the specific competence Fiber Optics builds, physical connectorization technique and system verification judgment, remains embodied and resistant to substitution in the central case through 2036, and the ABET-relevant sequence persists absent accreditor change. The honest uncertainty concerns how much of the design-and-budget analysis becomes AI-assisted, not whether students still need hands-on fiber-handling competence. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and by the course's specialized, hands-on character within the technology curriculum, even as the surrounding telecommunications field absorbs more AI-assisted planning and network-analysis tooling over the same period, and even as legacy protocols like FDDI and SONET recede further into a niche, still-taught body of systems knowledge.
EET 3690.d: Fiber optics is studied, including ray propagation, emitters, detectors, connectorization and systems, FDDI, and SONET.

r: This internship places juniors and seniors into a supervised professional placement in the field, arranged through the Classroom to Career Hub, with requirements that vary by placement. The applied work is whatever tasks the host employer assigns, likely a mix of engineering-support activities, some of which, documentation, data analysis, are more exposed to AI than others, equipment work, on-site troubleshooting, professional collaboration. What is not substitutable is the experiential core: supervised, embodied workplace practice and real-time professional judgment under an employer's direction, which task-exposure research does not treat as automatable. There is no course-specific licensure mandate, but the placement is a required professional-practice component of the accredited program. At 24 months the instrumental value of gaining direct workplace experience is essentially unaffected by AI's growing task competence elsewhere.

By 2031, AI tools will likely handle more of the administrative and analytical tasks interns are assigned, drafting documentation, summarizing data, supporting routine calculations, consistent with observed usage skewing toward office and computer-mathematical work. That plausibly narrows what interns spend time on, but the instrumental purpose of the course is supervised professional experience itself: learning to operate within a real engineering workplace, communicate with supervisors, and exercise judgment under real constraints. That experiential function is not something AI performs for the student. Employer expectations and the program's practice-based requirement persist across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low; some assigned tasks automate, but the course's core instrumental purpose does not erode with them, and firm-level survey data shows AI adoption still uneven across the small and mid-size employers that host many technology-program placements.

A decade out, AI will plausibly perform a larger share of the routine analytical and documentation tasks assigned to interns, and workplace roles may shift further toward oversight and collaboration with AI tools. But the central case still has engineering-technology programs requiring direct, supervised workplace exposure as part of professional formation, and that experiential, embodied requirement is not eliminated by task automation elsewhere in the job. The genuine uncertainty is in what specific tasks an intern is asked to do by 2036, not in whether supervised professional practice remains an instrumentally necessary component of the degree. The rating holds Low, reflecting the placement's experiential rather than task-execution purpose, a distinction the deterministic rule preserves regardless of how the surrounding labor market for engineering-support tasks evolves.
EET 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member within the major department, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: This course teaches a Hardware Description Language for designing and simulating large-scale digital integrated circuits, building on EET 3330. Writing HDL code is close kin to general programming, one of the most-exposed task categories in the evidence base, with controlled studies showing substantial AI-assisted coding speedups, and the work is entirely digital, offering no embodiment protection. AI already generates plausible HDL modules for well-specified problems. What holds the rating at Low for now is that verifying a synthesized design actually meets timing, area, and functional requirements before it reaches silicon carries real cost if wrong, and the course builds on the ABET-relevant sequence beginning with EET 2310 and EET 3330. At 24 months the instrumental need to learn HDL design fundamentals directly is still largely intact.

By 2031, AI HDL-generation tools will plausibly write substantial portions of well-specified digital-logic modules, consistent with the strong positive association between programming tasks and AI exposure and with rapid capability growth on coding benchmarks. The write-the-HDL-yourself rationale weakens considerably. What remains necessary is verifying that AI-generated HDL actually synthesizes correctly and meets specification, a high-stakes check given that flawed logic reaching fabrication is costly and errors can be non-obvious, the jagged-frontier problem in concentrated form. The ABET-relevant sequence this course sits within caps the erosion at Medium rather than allowing a rise to High. The rating moves to Medium: execution automates faster than verification competence becomes unnecessary, and the jagged-frontier evidence on mis-calibrated trust in AI output outside its reliable range is directly on point for a domain where a subtle logic error is expensive to catch after fabrication.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating most routine HDL modules and assisting substantially with verification tooling itself, and the manual-authorship rationale is largely eroded. But the ability to specify correct behavior, read simulation results critically, and catch a design that passes simulation yet fails in silicon remains a necessary human competence, and this course sits inside the ABET-relevant digital-design sequence that persists absent accreditor change. The rating holds Medium, capped from High by that structural role rather than by task-exposure, which by 2036 is genuinely high for HDL authorship. The uncertainty is in how HDL design work is organized around AI tools, not in whether foundational verification competence remains required for engineers who must sign off on a chip design before fabrication.
EET 4020.d: This course covers a Hardware Description Language (HDL) which is used to design and simulate very large scale digital integrated circuits.

r: This capstone course has student teams conceptualize, plan, and begin constructing an engineering design project in consultation with faculty advisors and industry contacts, applying fundamental engineering knowledge through hands-on prototyping. The applied work is physically embodied, building and initially testing hardware, coordinating a team, and working from real constraints, activities task-exposure research places outside AI's current reach even as AI assists with literature review or documentation drafting. Verifying that a proposed design will actually function once built requires hands-on engineering judgment, not AI's plausible-sounding output alone. ABET's engineering criteria call for exactly this kind of major design experience within the accredited sequence, though not this specific course by name. At 24 months the instrumental need for embodied, team-based design practice is essentially intact.

By 2031, AI will meaningfully assist with early-stage design ideation, documentation, and preliminary calculations, consistent with strong observed usage in computer-and-mathematical work. That plausibly compresses the planning phase of the project. What remains resistant is the embodied core: constructing and physically testing a working prototype under real engineering constraints, and exercising the judgment to know when a design idea, AI-generated or not, will not actually work. Verification burden is genuine here, since a flawed physical design has real consequences for the deliverable. The ABET-relevant capstone-design expectation persists across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low; AI reshapes the planning and documentation layer without displacing the hands-on design-and-build competence the course exists to teach, and the dampening effect of low embodiment and real verification stakes holds even as the surrounding planning work becomes more AI-assisted.

A decade out, AI design-assistance tools will likely generate more sophisticated preliminary concepts and simulations, and much of the early conceptualization workload may shift toward AI-human collaboration. But the embodied act of building, testing, and iterating a physical engineering deliverable under team and faculty guidance is not a task AI performs on the students' behalf, and ABET's major-design-experience expectation persists in the central case through 2036. The genuine uncertainty is how much conceptual design work happens with heavy AI assistance before physical construction begins, not whether the embodied capstone practice itself remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, consistent with the pattern across this catalog's other hands-on, build-and-verify project courses, and reflecting the low protective scores on both embodiment and verification burden that dampen the rating a full band below its raw task-exposure base.
EET 4100.d: This is a Senior Experience, capstone course designed to teach engineering design skills to students through project based learning. The course will focus on team project incorporating the application of fundamental engineering knowledge and skills. Projects requires planning and design in consultation with faculty advisors and industry contacts. Through this course the students will learn the design process in a hands on way through conceptualization, construction, testing and presenting a deliverable project.

r: In this second capstone course, teams complete, test, and demonstrate the project begun in EET 4100, producing written technical reports and oral presentations while consulting with a faculty advisor. The build-test-demonstrate work is physically embodied, assembling hardware, diagnosing why a prototype does not perform as designed, and validating a working deliverable, activities that sit outside AI's current reach even though AI can assist with report drafting, a more exposed writing task. Verifying that the finished project actually works as specified requires the student's own hands-on judgment; a plausible-looking simulation is not the same as a functioning device. ABET's design-experience expectations reinforce this hands-on, deliverable-based structure. At 24 months the instrumental need for embodied build-and-test competence, and for the professional communication skill of presenting it, is essentially intact.

By 2031, AI will draft and polish much of the written technical report and help structure the oral presentation, consistent with strong evidence that writing tasks are highly exposed and that AI assistance measurably improves professional-writing quality. That erodes the documentation portion of the course's rationale. The build-test-demonstrate core does not erode the same way: diagnosing why a physical prototype underperforms and validating that it meets specification remains embodied, hands-on troubleshooting work with real verification stakes. ABET's capstone-design expectations persist across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low; the reporting and presentation layer becomes more AI-assisted while the physical deliverable-validation core remains a distinctly human competence that anchors the overall rating, and the low embodiment and verification scores keep dampening it a full band below where task exposure alone would place it.

A decade out, AI will plausibly draft technical reports and presentation materials competently on demand, substantially eroding that component's instrumental rationale. But completing, testing, and validating a physical engineering deliverable, catching the gap between a simulated design and a device that must actually work, remains embodied troubleshooting that AI does not perform for the student, and ABET's major-design-experience expectation persists in the central case through 2036. The honest uncertainty is how much of the documentation and presentation preparation is AI-assisted by then, not whether the hands-on build-and-validate capstone competence remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, matching the pattern set by EET 4100 as its immediate predecessor course in this two-course capstone sequence, and reflecting the same low embodiment and verification-burden scores that dampen the rating a full band below its raw task-exposure base throughout.
EET 4110.d: In this course, the student completes the project he or she started in EET 4100. The project is built, tested, and demonstrated. Written technical reports and oral presentations on the project are required. Part of this course involves the student working with a faculty member who acts as a consultant.

r: The applied work is specifying and troubleshooting digital data-transmission systems, selecting synchronous versus asynchronous schemes, applying interface standards, sizing hardware, and diagnosing link errors. Parts of this sit squarely in the largest observed-usage category, Computer and Mathematical work, where AI already drafts configurations, decodes protocol standards, and explains framing or handshaking faults. But the course builds the engineer's competence to design and verify a working link end-to-end, and interpreting non-obvious failures such as timing skew, noise, and protocol mismatch is exactly where the jagged-frontier evidence shows unaided AI users go wrong with miscalibrated trust. The binding constraint is programmatic: as an ABET-accredited engineering-technology course it counts toward the accreditor's engineering-topic credit-hour floor, mandating the subject within the sequence. At 24 months adoption inside undergraduate EET is negligible and the instrumental need to learn data-communications design is intact. Rating Low.

By 2031 AI tooling will competently generate protocol configurations, auto-document interfaces, and propose fixes for common data-link faults, eroding the work-it-out-by-hand rationale for much routine data-communications practice. Task-exposure research places this technical, computer-centered work on the more-exposed side, and capability trends point toward steadily longer autonomous task horizons. The instrumental case shifts from producing configurations toward specifying requirements and verifying that an AI-proposed communication design actually meets timing, throughput, and standards constraints, verification burden the course's knowledge underwrites, since link failures are frequently non-obvious. ABET's engineering-topic credit-hour floor still mandates coverage of the subject across a catalog revision cycle, which caps erosion. The rating rises to Medium: the applied design work is increasingly automatable, but the accreditation lock and the residual need for a human who can validate the automated output keep the course from becoming instrumentally optional.

A decade out, the central case has AI handling most routine data-communications configuration and fault diagnosis, with the technologist's role centering on specifying, integrating, and validating automated designs rather than deriving them. The honest uncertainty is wide, since how deeply capable tooling actually diffuses into hands-on EET practice is unsettled, given that adoption has consistently lagged raw capability. What does not plausibly change by 2036 is ABET's requirement that an accredited program deliver engineering-topic content: the accreditation architecture moves slowly and continues to mandate the subject, holding the rating at Medium rather than High. Verification also remains load-bearing, because a technologist who cannot recognize a subtle protocol or timing failure cannot safely supervise AI-generated communication systems. Rating Medium, capped by the accreditation floor; the wide caveat concerns how the material is taught once AI drafts the configurations, not whether the competence remains instrumentally required.
EET 4330.d: This course covers methods of local and distant digital communications including: systems, standards, and hardware used for transmitting digital data either synchronously or asynchronously.

r: The applied work is interfacing computers with peripherals and other digital circuits, matching signal levels and logic families, mapping bus and I/O connections, handling handshaking and timing, and bench-debugging why two devices fail to communicate. Some of this is exposed: AI competently drafts glue-logic, explains datasheets, and suggests interface topologies, and observed-usage data confirms computer-and-mathematical work is the single most-used AI category. But the course develops embodied, hands-on competence, probing signals, reconciling a datasheet against actual circuit behavior, and resolving faults that are non-obvious in the way the jagged-frontier evidence flags as dangerous for unaided AI users. The binding constraint is the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor, which mandates this class of hardware content within the accredited EET sequence. At 24 months diffusion into undergraduate lab-bench practice is minimal and the instrumental need to learn hardware interfacing is undiminished. Rating Low.

By 2031 AI design aids will more capably generate interface circuitry, translate between device protocols, and propose debugging steps from datasheets, weakening the case for a student to work every interface out unaided. The technical, computer-adjacent portions sit on the more-exposed side of task-exposure research, and capability horizons keep lengthening. Yet interfacing retains a physical, bench-bound core, signal integrity, marginal timing, and hardware faults that surface only in the real circuit, so the instrumental value shifts toward specifying interfaces and verifying that an AI-proposed design behaves on actual silicon. That verification demand, plus the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor that still mandates the subject across a catalog cycle, caps erosion. Rating Medium: routine interface synthesis automates, but the embodiment of hardware bring-up and the accreditation lock keep the course from becoming instrumentally dispensable, even as the tooling absorbs more of the paper design.

Ten years out, the central case has AI generating most interface schematics and first-pass debugging guidance, with the technologist supervising, integrating, and validating on the bench. The uncertainty is genuine: physical hardware bring-up resists full automation, and adoption of capable tooling into hands-on EET work has trailed capability, so how much of this course's task actually gets displaced is unsettled. What holds firm is ABET's mandate that an accredited program teach engineering-topic hardware content; that accreditation lock changes on a slow cycle and keeps the rating at Medium rather than High through 2036. Verification stays essential, since a technologist who cannot diagnose a subtle signal-integrity or timing failure cannot trust an AI-generated interface in a deployed system. Rating Medium, bounded by accreditation and by the embodied, empirical nature of getting real hardware to talk; the caveat is about pedagogy under automation, not instrumental necessity.
EET 4340.d: This course covers interfacing techniques between computers, peripherals, and other digital circuits.

r: The course teaches microcontroller design, writing firmware, configuring monitor functions and hardware, managing timing, analog-to-digital conversion, and parallel and serial I/O. The programming component is among the most-exposed activities in the entire evidence base: coding is the largest observed-usage category and controlled studies show large developer speedups, so AI already drafts register-level code and peripheral configuration competently. But embedded work couples that code to physical timing, interrupts, and hardware constraints, where failures are non-obvious and the jagged-frontier evidence warns unaided AI users misjudge correctness. This course is also foundational scaffolding for later EET hardware courses such as Interface Techniques, and the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor mandates the subject in the accredited sequence. At 24 months, students cannot supervise or debug AI-generated firmware without understanding microcontroller fundamentals, and adoption into coursework is minimal. The instrumental need is intact. Rating Low.

By 2031 AI assistants will handle most routine firmware, generating peripheral drivers, interrupt skeletons, and I/O setup, pushing the write-it-yourself rationale further back, consistent with coding's strong positive exposure in the research and steadily lengthening autonomous task horizons. The instrumental case moves from authoring embedded code toward specifying behavior and verifying that AI-generated firmware meets real timing and hardware constraints, a verification competence this course builds and that matters because embedded failures are subtle and consequential. Its foundational role for downstream hardware courses and the ABET engineering-topic mandate both cap the erosion. Rating Medium: entry-level embedded implementation is increasingly automatable, but a technologist still needs the microcontroller fundamentals to direct and validate that automation, and the accreditation floor keeps the subject required across a catalog revision cycle. The shift is from writing firmware to owning its correctness, not from necessity to redundancy.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating most embedded firmware, with the technologist specifying, integrating, and verifying rather than hand-coding registers. The uncertainty is real, since how far capable tooling penetrates safety-relevant embedded practice, where verification burden is high, and how fast EET curricula adopt it, given diffusion has lagged capability, are both unsettled. What does not plausibly dissolve by 2036 is the course's role as substrate for higher-level hardware work and ABET's requirement that the accredited program teach it; those keep the rating at Medium rather than High. The conceptual foundation also remains necessary to catch the non-obvious firmware failures a model introduces, which is precisely the oversight competence the course develops. Rating Medium, capped by foundational role and accreditation; the wide caveat concerns how microcontroller design is taught when AI writes the code, not whether the underlying competence stays instrumentally required.
EET 4370.d: This course teaches microcontroller design. Topics include: programming, monitor functions, hardware configurations, timing, analog-to-digital conversion, parallel I/O, and serial I/O.

r: Unlike the design-oriented EET courses, this one has students research current and emerging electrical-engineering trends and analyze their societal impact, literature gathering, synthesis, and technical writing about where the field is heading. These are among the most AI-exposed activities anywhere: task-exposure research classifies writing as strongly positively associated with exposure, observed-usage data shows writing and office tasks prominent, and a professional-writing RCT found large time savings with quality gains. AI can already draft competent technology-trend surveys. The moderating factor is weaker here than for the hands-on courses, so the binding constraint is chiefly the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor, under which this course contributes to the accredited sequence. At 24 months, though, the base band from realized automatability lands at Medium and the accreditation cap pulls it to Low; classroom adoption is early and the course's synthesis-and-judgment aim is not yet displaced. Rating Low.

By 2031 AI will fluently produce technology-trend research and societal-impact analysis end-to-end, retrieving sources, synthesizing developments, and drafting polished prose, which erodes the instrumental case for a student to do the survey work unaided more sharply than for this program's design courses. Verification burden is comparatively modest, since claims about trends are checkable and error cost is low, so little protects the rating from below except structure. What caps it is the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor, which still mandates the course's place in the accredited curriculum across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium accordingly. The residual instrumental value lies in a student developing the judgment to frame questions, weigh sources, and critically appraise emerging technology rather than accept AI-generated synthesis uncritically, a real but narrowing rationale as the underlying research-and-writing tasks become increasingly automatable.

Ten years out, the central case has AI competently producing most of what this course asks, trend identification, impact analysis, and technical writeups, leaving the human contribution centered on judgment, critical appraisal, and asking the right questions. Absent the embodiment or high verification burden that protect the design courses, the main thing holding the rating off High is the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor, whose slow revision cycle keeps the subject inside the accredited sequence through 2036. My confidence is lower here than for the hands-on courses, because whether a societal-impact research elective is counted and retained as engineering-topic content is more contestable than for a circuits or microcontroller course. Rating Medium, held by the accreditation cap; the honest caveat is that if that structural mandate loosened, this is the EET course whose instrumental rationale would erode fastest under highly capable research-and-writing automation.
EET 4700.d: This course identifies and researches current and emerging trends, topics, and developments in the field of electrical engineering to determine their impact on society and to identify changes in the society that could result from these new developments.

r: The applied work is designing digital control systems using classical and modern theory, deriving feedback control laws, placing poles, and designing state-variable controllers and observers. Symbolic and computational steps are exposed to AI, which can manipulate transfer functions, run design math, and generate controller code; observed-usage data confirms computer-and-mathematical work is the most-used AI category. But control design leans on the scientific and critical-thinking skills that task-exposure research finds strongly negatively associated with exposure, and its failures, instability and poor robustness, are non-obvious and potentially dangerous, exactly the jagged-frontier condition demanding a knowledgeable human check. The binding constraint is the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor mandating this content in the accredited EET sequence. At 24 months the instrumental need to understand control-system design is intact: a student cannot validate an AI-proposed controller for stability and performance without the theory. Rating Low.

By 2031 AI tools will more capably synthesize controllers, tune gains, and generate implementation code, weakening the case for a student to derive every design by hand. The computational portions are exposed, but the interpretive core, judging stability margins, robustness, and whether a control law is safe to deploy, carries heavy verification burden, because control failures are consequential and non-obvious, so the human competence remains necessary for oversight. The instrumental case shifts from deriving controllers toward specifying performance requirements and validating AI-generated designs against them. ABET's engineering-topic credit-hour floor still mandates the subject across a catalog revision cycle, capping erosion. Rating Medium: routine control-law synthesis automates, yet the verification demands intrinsic to feedback design and the accreditation lock keep the course instrumentally required. What changes is that graduates increasingly certify and integrate AI-proposed controllers rather than compute them from scratch, not that the underlying competence becomes optional.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating most control-system designs, with the technologist specifying objectives, integrating, and, critically, verifying stability and robustness before anything actuates real hardware. Uncertainty is genuine on how far automation penetrates safety-relevant control practice, where an unnoticed instability is costly, and on how fast EET programs adopt such tooling given diffusion lags. What does not plausibly change by 2036 is ABET's mandate that an accredited program teach engineering-topic design content; that slow-moving accreditation lock holds the rating at Medium rather than High. The verification argument also persists: certifying an AI-designed controller as safe requires exactly the control theory this course builds, and the science-and-critical-thinking core sits in the lower-exposure band. Rating Medium, capped by accreditation and sustained by verification burden; the caveat concerns how control design is taught under automation, not whether it remains instrumentally necessary.
EET 4710.d: Students in this course will learn the process and theory of the design of digital control systems, using classical and modern control theory. State variable feedback control laws and observers are designed.

r: The course covers robot design, analysis, modeling, and control, forward and inverse kinematics, kinetics, sensor and actuator selection, and industrial applications. The mathematical modeling is partly exposed: AI can solve kinematic equations, derive Jacobians, and generate control code, and observed-usage data confirms computer-and-mathematical work is the largest AI-use category. But robotics couples that analysis to physical actuation, sensing, and safety, where failures are non-obvious and the jagged-frontier evidence warns of miscalibrated trust in unaided AI output; the scientific reasoning involved is the kind task-exposure research finds negatively associated with exposure. The binding constraint is the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor mandating this content in the accredited EET sequence. At 24 months the instrumental need to understand how robots are modeled and controlled is intact, since a student cannot validate an AI-generated kinematic or control solution against real actuators without the underlying theory. Rating Low.

By 2031 AI will more capably derive kinematic models, plan trajectories, and generate robot-control code, eroding the case for a student to work each derivation unaided. The analytical portions are exposed, but robotics retains a physical, safety-critical core, a mis-modeled joint or unsafe trajectory has real-world consequences, so verification burden keeps a knowledgeable human necessary, and the instrumental value shifts toward specifying robot behavior and validating AI-proposed models and controllers on actual hardware. ABET's engineering-topic credit-hour floor still mandates the subject across a catalog revision cycle, capping erosion. Rating Medium: routine kinematic and control synthesis becomes automatable, yet the embodiment of real actuation and the verification demands of safe robot operation, together with the accreditation lock, keep the course instrumentally required. Graduates increasingly integrate and certify AI-designed robotic systems rather than derive them from scratch, but the competence itself is not displaced.

Ten years out, the central case has AI generating most robot modeling, motion planning, and control code, with the technologist specifying tasks, integrating subsystems, and verifying safe physical behavior. The uncertainty is wide: robotics that touches the physical world resists full automation and its verification burden is high, while adoption of advanced tooling into hands-on EET instruction has trailed raw capability. What does not plausibly change by 2036 is ABET's requirement that an accredited program deliver engineering-topic design content; that slow accreditation cycle holds the rating at Medium rather than High. The verification case also persists, since certifying an AI-designed robotic system as safe demands the kinematics and control theory this course builds, competencies in the lower-exposure scientific band. Rating Medium, bounded by accreditation and by the embodied, safety-critical nature of real robots; the caveat is about pedagogy under automation, not whether the competence remains instrumentally necessary.
